drills.q: A text response passes every output filter clean, but a customer's SSN still leaked. What's the first thing you check?
drills.a: Whether the SSN left through a tool call, API write, or log line the output filter never inspected, since output guardrails typically only scan the final chat text.

drills.q: Rank these by typical added latency: Guardrails AI ML validator, schema/regex check, LLM-based validator.
drills.a: Schema/regex (<10ms) < Guardrails AI ML validator (50-200ms) < LLM-based validator (200-800ms).

drills.q: Your guardrail catches 90% of serious problems but has a 25% false-positive rate. Is this a good tradeoff for a consumer product?
drills.a: Likely not — a 25% FP rate is well above the 5-15% industry range and will generate daily friction; under pressure the threshold typically gets loosened, eroding even the 90% catch rate over time.

drills.q: A PII-detection microservice goes down. Your product is an internal engineering chatbot with no external users and no regulated data. Fail-open or fail-closed, and why?
drills.a: Fail-open — low-stakes, no regulated data, availability matters more than the marginal risk from one unchecked response in this domain.

drills.q: Same scenario, but the product is a healthcare intake assistant. Fail-open or fail-closed?
drills.a: Fail-closed — regulated, high-stakes domain; if you can't prove the output is safe, don't send it, even at the cost of an outage.

drills.q: Which guardrail layer specifically targets hallucination in a RAG system, and what does it check?
drills.a: Groundedness checking — it verifies that claims in the response trace back to the retrieved source documents.

drills.q: A teammate proposes running an LLM-as-judge output validator on every single turn of a high-traffic product. What's your pushback with numbers?
drills.a: That adds 200-800ms latency and roughly 15-40% to the provider bill per turn on every request; route it instead to only high-stakes or RAG-backed categories rather than applying it as a blanket per-turn gate.

drills.q: Your jailbreak detector had a great benchmark score at launch a year ago. Attack success rate has crept up since. Why, without any code change?
drills.a: Jailbreak classifiers are adversarial targets; attackers iterate against known detectors the way they iterate against WAF rules, so effectiveness decays as new phrasings are discovered even with a static model.

drills.q: Design the output-side guardrail stack for a RAG customer-support agent, in priority order, and justify the order.
drills.a: PII redaction and schema validation first (cheap, always relevant), then groundedness check against retrieved sources as the highest-priority expensive layer, since the dominant risk in a support bot is confidently wrong information, ahead of toxicity classification.

drills.q: Why is 'add a guardrail' not a complete answer in a design review?
drills.a: Because guardrails are layered and each catches a different failure at a different cost; the answer needs to name which layer, what it specifically catches and misses, and its latency/cost budget.

drills.q: A support bot's topical-restriction guardrail blocks 12% of legitimate messages in its first week. What's the likely operational failure mode if nothing changes?
drills.a: Complaint volume pressures someone to loosen the threshold in a hotfix, and the threshold is often never re-tightened once complaints stop, silently eroding the protection back toward zero.

drills.q: Give one case where adding a cheap, available guardrail layer is still the wrong call.
drills.a: When it duplicates coverage a stronger control already provides (e.g., a text-response PII filter on a system where the agent has no tool capable of leaking PII), since it only adds false-positive risk with no matching threat.
